dek: A handicapper known from Proline, Sports Central radio and The Winning Edge who sold picks from 1982 until 2022. He died on 7 Sep 2022 at 68. His last sales page, on Big Al, is gone; we found no Larry Ness package on sale today, no full record of his picks, and forum opinion that splits between respect and distrust.

short_answer: Larry Ness was a real and well known handicapper. His obituary says he began in 1982 with Las Vegas handicapper Jim Feist, appeared on Feist's USA Network show Proline, and hosted a syndicated radio show from the Bally's sportsbook from 1990. He later joined Wayne Root's Winning Edge and sold picks online for many years, last through Big Al's site. He died on 7 Sep 2022 at 68.

We found no Larry Ness package for sale on 20 Nov 2026. His Big Al profile address now redirects to the home page, and he is not on that site's handicapper list. If you see his name on a sales page today, ask who is making the picks.

Whether his picks made money over his career is something nobody can now check. His last sales page listed strong seasons, such as 144-108-7 in the NFL across 2018 and 2019, but those are seller figures for chosen windows, and the dollar profits shown are about nine to ten times what the same records make at flat stakes. His best known credential, a 1985 Castaways contest win, was publicly disputed by another handicapper days after his death. Forum opinion over 15 years splits about evenly.

guarantee: We found no guarantee terms for Larry Ness, because we found no current sales page. Any guarantee he offered in the past would have been set by the site selling his picks.
His 2000 site carried a disclaimer that its information was "for entertainment purposes and news matter only" and that the business could not be held liable for the content or its accuracy.
As with every pick service, losses on the bets themselves are never covered, and they are usually far larger than any package price.

claims.claim: "back to back seasons (2018 & 2019) of going a combined 144-108-7, earning a profit of $22,458 at $100/unit"
claims.status: Checked the arithmetic: 57.1% winners. At flat $100 bets and -110 that record makes about $2,520, so the $22,458 figure assumes much larger stakes on his higher star plays, about nine times flat. Seller figure, no full log

claims.claim: "from 2019 Week 4 thru the Super Bowl, Larry's top rated NFL 10*s went 31-13, or 70.5% ATS"
claims.status: Arithmetic checks: 31 of 44 is 70.5%. The window starts at Week 4, a date chosen by the seller

Checked: 58.4% and 55.7%. At flat $100 and -110 these make about $1,580 and $860, so the dollar totals again depend on star sized stakes. The same page admits he "stumbled" in 2019 college football and had an "off year" in 2019-20 college hoops

claims.claim: His NHL "Big Plays" were "18-7 (72%)" and he "earned a profit in SEVEN of the last 10" MLB seasons
claims.status: 18 of 25 is 72%, so the arithmetic checks. Winning seasons count periods, not money; no season totals were shown

claims.status: Disputed by another handicapper in Sep 2022 who says he made the winning picks; unresolved

claims.status: Consistent with his obituary, which dates his start to 1982 with Jim Feist

claims_note: How we checked: the Big Al profile saved on 25 May 2022 listed his recent seasons with records and dollar profits. We worked out each win rate and what the record would earn betting a flat $100 at -110. Every dollar figure is about nine to ten times the flat result, which fits a service that rated plays from 6 to 10 stars and sized bets by stars. That is a legitimate way to report, but a buyer betting the same amount on every play would have made far less.
The windows are selective. The NFL figure covers two chosen seasons, and the 10 star run starts at Week 4 of 2019. To the page's credit, it also named losing seasons, which most sales pages do not.

The 1985 contest claim is the clearest problem. Three days after his death, Gambling911 published a veteran handicapper's account that he, not Ness, made the picks for that winning entry, which he says was entered as Top Play Sports with Jim Feist paying the fee, and that Ness was a paid front man; both men, he said, worked at Feist's National Sports Services. Ness could not respond, and Gambling911 said the question was "to be determined." We found no follow up.
The kind words in the obituary and eulogy come from friends and business partners. They are fair to report, but they are not a record.
record: What a buyer can verify independently: nothing that we could find. We found no full, time stamped log of every Larry Ness pick, no audited monitor record we could open, and no court or regulator record about him.

What the seller side published: selected seasons and streaks on the Big Al profile up to 2022, and earlier sites that showed daily free picks and notes but, by a 2007 forum account, no archive of past picks.

What was said publicly: a 2007 TheRX member posted a 162-82 record for that year without a source, and a 2022 Sportsbook Review member noted that his last listed pick, a White Sox bet, won. Neither is a full record.

Business history: in 2000 he sold Game of the Day picks as Larry Ness' Sports Marketplace from an address in Hauppauge, New York, and hosted a Monday night show at Gilley's in the New Frontier casino in Las Vegas. By 2006 his site carried a Covers Media Group copyright and a toll free sales line. In Oct 2020 a paid press release from GoooGreen Inc. named him on the panel of its new VegasWINNERS subsidiary led by Wayne Allyn Root. His obituary says he lived in Las Vegas from 1982, in Malibu and Santa Monica from 2000 to 2011, back in Las Vegas until 2014, and then in Homosassa, Florida.

our_data.text: Watchdog grades picks captured from public posts before the game starts. In this edition no Larry Ness pick history is matched to a Watchdog graded record, so we make no claim about how Larry Ness performed.
our_data.context: For scale: the seasons listed on his last sales page ran from about 56% to 58% winners. On the Watchdog board, {{over60}} of {{established}} established accounts (100 or more graded picks) were at 60% or better, and the median established account won {{median_win}}% of its picks. At standard -110 odds a bettor needs about 52.4% to break even.

customers_intro: Independent comment on Larry Ness comes from three forum threads, one from 2007 and two written the week he died in 2022. None includes a receipt or a full record. Below is what we found, positive and negative, and how much weight it can carry.

customers.text: We read about 30 opinion posts across three threads on TheRX, Covers and Sportsbook Review, from 2007 and 2022, plus tribute pages on sites that sold or promoted him. Forum opinion splits close to evenly. Supporters say he was respected, did his own research, bet his own money and had good stretches, and a 2007 member credited him with only three losing football weeks in sixteen. Critics say his records could not be checked because his site kept no archive, that he was a name on the label rather than the person picking, and that his biggest plays were worth betting against. Several posts are general complaints about all touts rather than about him. Nobody in these threads posted a receipt or a season of results from buying his picks, we found no post about him in Reddit searches, and the pick sites that praised him (Big Al, BoydsBets, a VegasWINNERS press release) sold or promoted his picks, so they are not independent.

In a TheRX thread about his plays, one member called him one of the biggest frauds in the business and said to bet against him, and another claimed he did not pick the games himself and that his name was what sold. Neither gave evidence.
In the same thread, other members called him a good handicapper who picks winners, said he was having a great year, and one posted a 162-82 record for the year without a source.

One member said his recent results looked good but that his website had no archive of past picks, so he would not buy. Another said he bet a lot of favorites but had only three losing weeks in sixteen.

On Sportsbook Review the week he died, one member said a profile calling him honest could not be verified but matched his reputation, and described him as someone who researched his picks and bet his own money. Another called him a respected figure in the business.
In the same thread, one member doubted he was ever a sharp or winning bettor, but credited his convincing on air style.

On Covers, one member said he profited for years by betting against Ness's top plays and called him a scammer, and another described his handicapping as mediocre at best. A third member in the same thread called him one of the best handicappers. None gave records.

His Big Al profile quoted him saying his work product speaks for itself and that the Larry Ness brand was instantly recognizable after 37 years. The page listed winning seasons and streaks and named two off years. Big Al sold his picks, so this is seller material.

BoydsBets, a pick selling site, keeps a tribute page calling him one of the sharpest minds its writer knew, describing his matchup based approach and early release times. It names no records beyond the disputed 1985 contest.

We found no current Larry Ness sales page: the Big Al profile now redirects to the home page and he is not on its handicapper list. Reddit searches for his name in r/sportsbook found no post about him.

conflicts: The most generous accounts of his career come from Wayne Root, his longtime business partner, from Big Al, which sold his picks, and from BoydsBets, a pick seller. They are fair to report but not independent.

In 2020 he was named in a paid press release for VegasWINNERS, a Wayne Root company then a subsidiary of GoooGreen Inc., a company quoted on the OTC Pink market, alongside other handicappers it sold. Release copy is marketing, not a record.
The 1985 contest claim that appeared on sales pages was disputed by another handicapper who says he made the picks for that entry. The dispute was never settled in anything we found.
strengths: A real, documented career on national handicapping TV and radio over two decades, confirmed by an independent obituary.
Some independent forum members describe him as respected and as someone who researched games and bet his own picks.
His last sales page explained his star ratings, release times and play types in detail, so buyers knew what they were getting.
That page named losing seasons as well as winning ones, which is rare in pick marketing.
Early prices were modest, such as $29.95 for 30 days of Game of the Day picks in 2000.
concerns: Died in Sep 2022. Any product sold under his name today would be made by someone else.
No full public record of his picks was ever found, and one 2007 forum member said his site kept no archive.
The dollar profits on his sales page are about nine to ten times what the same records make at flat stakes, because they rely on star sized bets, and the windows were chosen by the seller.
His headline contest credential is publicly disputed.
Forum opinion is split, and the negative posts include allegations that he fronted for picks made by others. These are allegations without evidence.
checklist: If any site sells picks under the Larry Ness name, ask who makes them and when that person started.
Ask any seller for every pick from the last 12 months with the line, the odds and the time it was sent. A list of hot runs is not a record.
When a record is shown in dollars, ask what stake each star rating means and work out the flat stake result yourself.
Read the guarantee for the words refund, credit and extension. Most "guarantees" in this business are credits.
Write down each pick yourself the moment you receive it, with the line you can actually get.
Give any handicapper a few hundred picks before you call them a winner. Short runs swing hard both ways.
faq: He was a real, long running TV and radio handicapper who sold picks for about 40 years. He died on 7 Sep 2022, and we found no current Larry Ness package for sale. We could not verify his long run record, and we found no court or regulator action involving him.
How much does Larry Ness cost?

There is no current price, because no sales page under his name was live on 20 Nov 2026. Historical prices on his own sites included $29.95 for 30 days of Game of the Day picks in 2000 and $399 for a month of college basketball picks in 2006.
Does Larry Ness have a verified record?

No. We found no full, time stamped record of his picks. His last sales page showed chosen seasons, such as 144-108-7 in the NFL across 2018 and 2019, and his 1985 Castaways contest win was disputed by another handicapper in 2022.
Where did Larry Ness sell his picks?

Through his own sites from at least 2000, first as Larry Ness' Sports Marketplace and later at larrynesssports.com, and in his last years through Big Al's pick site. A 2020 press release also named him on the VegasWINNERS panel.
What do bettors say about Larry Ness?

Opinion is split. Some forum members called him respected and said he bet his own picks; others called him a front man or said his top plays were worth fading. Nobody we found posted a full record either way.
Is anyone still selling Larry Ness picks?
Not that we found. His Big Al profile now redirects to the home page. If a site uses his name now, the picks come from someone else, so judge that person's own record.
